requirement:
# REQ-2297: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2297

#### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.
MessagePack generated code is not decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.

Because it is very hard to write good coverage for generated MessagePack code, it may skew coverage numbers, especially on large projects with a lot of generated code.

#### Describe the solution you'd like
I would like all generated code to be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.  I do not feel like a setting is needed, but setting would be fine to have too.

#### Describe alternatives you've considered
There are no alternatives, it is close to impossible to write good coverage for generated code as it covers many edge cases.

#### Additional context

N/A

story.summary: The source generator templates now put `[global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` on each generated type. That covers the object formatter (int-keyed and string-keyed), enum, union, the generated resolver and its nested `FormatterCache<T>` / `GetFormatterHelper` classes, and the composite resolver and its `FormatterCache<T>`. Every attribute is wrapped in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. A one-line fix in TransformUtilities emits a line break after `{` when nesting types have constraints, so the `#if` lands at the start of a line. The 222 snapshot files were regenerated, and a README note and a new two-test file were added.
story.why: The issue asks that all generated code carry ExcludeFromCodeCoverage so it does not skew coverage numbers.
touches_beyond_requirement: TransformUtilities.cs line 58 changes the generated whitespace for every nested type with generic constraints. It is needed so the `#if` directive starts a line, but it alters output that was not otherwise touched.
README.md gains a doc note. Its claim that the attribute is unavailable on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework appears to be wrong.
The `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` guard is the agent's own design decision. It is not in the requirement, and it narrows who gets the feature.

Low on the guard premise: ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute ships in .NET Framework 4.0+ and in netstandard2.0, so consumers on those targets get no exclusion. Medium on the new tests: they check per file, not per type, and they never compile the generated code. The 222 snapshots were only sampled (2 shown), and the uniformity check S2 fails with 7 shapes.

claims.text: When a nesting type has generic constraints, EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces now writes `{` followed by a line break. Previously it wrote a bare `{`, so the next `#if` directive would have started mid-line. This changes only whitespace in generated output.

The README documents that generated formatters and resolvers carry the attribute, and that it is skipped on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework. The stated reason, that it is unavailable there, appears to be factually wrong.

Test AllGeneratedTypesAreExcludedFromCodeCoverage runs the generator on a source with int-keyed, string-keyed, enum, union and resolver types. claims.text: Test ExcludeAttributeIsGuardedForTargetsWhereItIsUnavailable asserts two things for each generated file: there is at least one attribute, and every occurrence sits inside the exact `#if`/`#endif` guard block (tab-indented or not). It counts occurrences with the CountOccurrences helper.

Shared test setup works in three parts. The constants define the expected attribute and guard strings. RunGeneratorAsync builds a compilation against the default framework and MessagePack references. It then runs MessagePackGenerator and returns each generated tree's path and text, discarding diagnostics and the updated compilation.

The sampled regenerated snapshots show the guarded attribute exactly where the templates place it. In the formatter snapshot that is above the nested formatter. In the resolver snapshot it is above the resolver class, FormatterCache and GetFormatterHelper. The remaining 220 snapshots were not shown, and S2 reports 7 distinct change shapes.

findings.description: The `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` guard (repeated in all six templates) rests on a false premise. System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute exists in .NET Framework 4.0+ and in .NET Standard 2.0, and can be applied to classes there. Consumers on those targets get no exclusion, which defeats 'all generated code' for a large share of users (netstandard libraries, Unity, net4x apps).

The attribute is placed on `partial class <ResolverName>`, which the user also declares. ExcludeFromCodeCoverage is AllowMultiple=false. A user who already put [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] on their partial resolver, a natural workaround for this exact issue, now gets error CS0579 'Duplicate attribute'. The same applies to the composite resolver (CompositeResolverTemplate.tt line 8). Nested formatter, cache and helper classes are generator-only and unaffected.
The docs state the attribute is 'not available' on netstandard2.0 / .NET Framework. This appears to be incorrect and would mislead users.

`text.Contains(ExcludeAttribute)` passes if any one type in a file has the attribute. The resolver file has three types, so a missing attribute on FormatterCache or GetFormatterHelper would go undetected. This contradicts the test's summary ('every type').

Generator diagnostics and the output compilation are discarded. The tests never verify that the generated code with the attribute and directives compiles. TestSource has no composite resolver and no generic-constrained nested type, so C6 and C7 rely only on existing snapshot tests not shown in the diff.
The guard test locks in the questionable TFM exclusion. Removing the guard to fix the first concern would fail this test.
S2 Generated snapshot files change uniformly: 222 generated file(s); 7 distinct changed line shape(s) (too varied to be one mechanical change)

out_of_scope.description: Whitespace change to nesting-type emission. It is needed so the `#if` lands on its own line, but it alters generated output for all constrained nested types.
Documentation note. It contains an inaccurate availability claim.
